detail: Directors face personal liability for company debts if they make a false Declaration of Solvency in an MVL, with potential criminal sanctions under section 89(4) of the Insolvency Act 1986.

HMRC can use the 'Transactions in Securities' rules (sections 684 to 703, Income Tax Act 2007) to reclassify MVL distributions as income if the purpose was tax avoidance rather than a genuine winding up, especially when followed by a new company in the same trade.
The Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rule (TAAR), introduced in 2016, can reclassify MVL distributions as income (not capital gains) if the same trade is resumed through a new company within two years.
Distributions from an MVL are treated as capital for tax purposes and may qualify for Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) at 10% on the first £1 million of qualifying gains.
HMRC can apply the 'Transactions in Securities' rules to reclassify MVL distributions as income if the purpose was tax avoidance rather than a genuine winding up.
The Declaration of Solvency must be made within five weeks before the winding-up resolution is passed.
A shareholders' special resolution to wind up the company and appoint a liquidator must be passed within five weeks of the Declaration of Solvency.
The winding-up resolution must be advertised in the London Gazette within 14 days of being passed.
The liquidator must notify Companies House of their appointment within 15 days of the winding-up resolution.
A straightforward MVL typically completes in 6 to 12 months from the date of the shareholders' resolution.
The company is formally dissolved approximately three months after the liquidator files the final return with Companies House.
Directors are required to cooperate fully with the liquidator, providing all requested documents and information, as per Section 235 of the Insolvency Act 1986.
If a company's distributable reserves are below £25,000, dissolution may be a simpler route than an MVL.
The 'phoenixing for tax purposes' rule can reclassify MVL distributions as income if the director liquidates one company and immediately starts a new one doing the same work.
The Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rule (TAAR) applies if a director continues to carry on the same trade through a new company within two years of an MVL.
An overdrawn Director's Loan Account (DLA) is treated as a debt owed to the company, which the liquidator must pursue for creditors.
If an overdrawn DLA is not repaid within nine months of the company's year-end, the company may incur a Section 455 tax charge (currently 33.75%).
An overdrawn DLA exceeding £10,000 without interest can attract a benefit-in-kind tax for the director.
If a director continues to withdraw money from an overdrawn DLA when the company is insolvent, it could be treated as wrongful trading or misfeasance.

HMRC can issue Joint and Several Liability Notices (JSLNs) making directors personally liable for company tax debts in specific circumstances, including repeated insolvencies and tax liabilities exceeding £10,000.

HMRC can issue Personal Liability Notices (PLNs) under Section 121C of the Social Security Administration Act 1992, making directors personally liable for unpaid National Insurance Contributions if the underpayment was due to their fraud or neglect.

detail: Since 1 December 2020, HMRC is a secondary preferential creditor for certain taxes, including VAT, PAYE Income Tax, and Employee National Insurance Contributions.
A company can be restored to the register for up to six years after dissolution for creditors to pursue debts.
HMRC can apply to restore a company to the register for up to 20 years if tax is owed.
The Insolvency Service can investigate directors of dissolved companies without restoration, as of February 2022.
Section 239 of the Insolvency Act 1986 allows liquidators to apply to reverse transactions where one creditor was unfairly preferred.
Challenging preferences under Section 239 Insolvency Act 1986 has a two-year relevant time window for connected parties (e.g., directors) and six months for unconnected parties.
Wrongful trading, as defined by Section 214 of the Insolvency Act 1986, occurs when directors continue trading when they knew or ought to have known the company could not avoid insolvent liquidation.
Directors found guilty of wrongful trading can be ordered to contribute personally to the company's assets under Section 214 of the Insolvency Act 1986.
Directors disqualified for wrongful trading may face periods of 2 to 15 years under the Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986.
Section 216 of the Insolvency Act 1986 prohibits directors of liquidated companies from being involved with another company using a 'prohibited name' for five years.
Breaching Section 216 of the Insolvency Act 1986 (prohibited name use) can result in imprisonment and/or a fine.
Section 217 of the Insolvency Act 1986 can make directors personally liable for the debts of a new company using a prohibited name.
The Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 can disqualify directors for periods of 2 to 15 years for unfit conduct.
The Insolvency Service can seek compensation orders against disqualified directors to pay for losses to creditors.
Acting as a director while disqualified is a criminal offence, potentially carrying imprisonment of up to two years and/or a fine.
The cost of a straightforward MVL can range from £995 + VAT and expenses to £3,000 + VAT.
More complex MVLs, involving physical assets or outstanding liabilities, can incur fees ranging from £1,995 to £6,000 + VAT and expenses.
Factors influencing MVL costs include complexity of assets, number of directors/shareholders, outstanding liabilities, HMRC tax claims, and property transfers.
MVL fees are comprised of the Liquidator's professional fees and disbursements, such as statutory advertising and the liquidator's insurance bond.
The costs of an MVL are paid out of the company's assets, not by the directors personally.
Voluntary strike-off and dissolution may be suitable for dormant companies with minimal assets and no ongoing liabilities.
A voluntary strike-off application to Companies House costs £8 online or £44 by post.
For a company to be eligible for strike-off, it must not have traded, sold stock, changed its name, or been threatened with liquidation in the last three months.
If a company is dissolved with undistributed assets, these assets may pass to the Crown as bona vacantia.
A Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA) is a legally binding agreement between an insolvent company and its creditors to propose a debt repayment plan.
In Administration, the primary objectives are to rescue the company as a going concern or achieve a better outcome for creditors than liquidation.
Administrative receivers are appointed by a secured creditor to recover money for that specific creditor.
If a company is insolvent, it must convert an MVL to a Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL).
The Declaration of Solvency requires directors to include pending tax returns, potential warranty claims, dilapidation provisions, and any deferred consideration from past transactions.
Directors must include contingent and prospective liabilities when assessing the company's balance sheet for the Declaration of Solvency.
The MVL process must include obtaining formal clearance from HMRC regarding PAYE, VAT, and Corporation Tax.
In an MVL, directors have a duty to cooperate fully with the liquidator, providing requested documents and information under Section 235 of the Insolvency Act 1986.
